title: Impact of Political Turnover on Public Spending

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy
We will use an Instrumental Variable (IV) approach to identify the causal effect of Democratic control on public spending. The key instrument here is the close-election Democratic win (`z`). The core assumption for the IV strategy is the exclusion restriction, which implies that `z` affects public spending only through `x` (Democratic control), and not through any other pathway. Additionally, `z` is assumed to be strongly correlated with `x` (relevance condition).

## 2. R Code
```r
# Load necessary packages
library(AER)
library(readr)

# Read the dataset
data <- read_csv("experiments/exp_b/data/s74_data.csv")

# Run the IV regression
iv_model <- ivreg(y ~ x + controls | z + controls, data = data)

# Summarize the results
summary(iv_model)

# Check the first-stage regression (relevance)
first_stage <- lm(x ~ z + controls, data = data)
summary(first_stage)

# Endogeneity test (Durbin-Wu-Hausman test)
dw_test <- phtest(iv_model, lm(y ~ x + controls, data = data))
print(dw_test)
```

## 3. Expected Findings
The expected sign of the coefficient on `x` (Democratic control) is positive, indicating that a Democratic control leads to an increase in public spending. The magnitude would typically depend on the extent of spending priorities under Democratic control versus alternatives, but a modest positive coefficient is commonly hypothesized in similar literatures due to platform policies typically favoring increased public spending. Since this is an IV approach addressing potential endogeneity with elections, we anticipate more robust estimates compared to OLS. The exact magnitude would rely on historical spending trends post-election victories.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: Use close-election Democratic wins as an instrument for Democratic control.
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: The analysis suggests a negative causal impact of Democratic control on public spending.
